content.summary_of_the_paper: This work addressed the task of attacking and defending vision-language models. It adopts a query-based attack model, i.e., sending a text (or image) query to the victim model and collecting the returned image (or text) that forms a image-text pair. The collected pairs are used as the training data for obtaining a local copy of the victim V-L models.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
- The topic (security of AI models) is increasingly crucial in recent years.
- The empirical investigation is quite comprehensive, including various ablation studies (e.g., replacing the neural backbones or varying the query number) and analysis (e.g., analyze which types of queries are most effective). 

Weakness:
- The technical contribution is very limited. The attack is conducted in a standard way - sending query to the victim model, collecting sufficiently many returned "samples", and eventually training a surrogate model which mimics the victim model's behavior.
- The goal is to attack vision-language model. However, except for using image-text pairs rather than only images, there are hardly many designs specifically for the vision-language model.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: All key concepts, technical details ang experiments are presented in a clear way. I have no complaint regarding the writing.
Quality: Although appreciating the excellent writing and extensive experiments, I would regard some claims misleading (see my detailed comment in the next section) and the overall technical contributions are not significant enough.
Novelty: Not significant enough.
Reproducibility: There seem no hidden engineering tricks in the proposed method, thus I would believe readers can re-implement it with reasonable effort.
content.summary_of_the_review:
I have several concerns regarding this work that make me hesitate to recommend acceptance. Though the target model in the experiments is CLIP-style pre-trained vision-language model, the attack is actually on a "finetuned" version. In other words, the success is defined by mimicking the behavior of the original CLIP model, but a simplified version on specific data distribution (e.g., MSCOCO). On the other hand, the number of queries used for training the local copy is huge. In most experiments, the original training data is split into two equal subsets. One is used for finetuning the original CLIP model, and the other half is used as queries. All above facts collectively make the attack not so challenging. 

The attack methodology is a conventional one, by constructing a training set via querying the victim model. There is not novel insight with regard to attack / defense methods. This further lowers the significance of the technical contributions.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper studies an interesting problem that the pretrained large-scale vision language model could be stealed by query attacks. They conduct experimental results on two image-text retrieval datasets and found the surrogate model could achieve similar performance to the original models.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength
1. The introduced problem is new in the vision language area.
2. The paper is well-organized and very easy to follow.

Weakness
1. The proposed setting still is not reasonable. The large-scale pretrained vision language model usually runs in several areas, including text-image retrieval, image question answering, image captioning, and image classification. However, only the retrieval task is studied in this work. 
2. In addition, the surrogate model can not be initialized with pre-trained vision weights.  When no pertaining datasets are feasible, how the stealing attack achieves comparable performance with the fine-tuned model which uses pertaining weights?
3. The defense idea is borrowed from previous works. What is the contribution in the current manuscript?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The idea is clearly delivered.
There are no new proposed methods or significant findings in the paper.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper introduces an interesting problem in vision language learning. However, the proposed setting is incompleted and experiments are not well conducted to validate the claims. Therefore, I tend to reject the current paper.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper focuses on stealing the functionality of VLP (vision-language pre-training) models that are fine-tuned on image-text retrieval tasks. This paper assumes that the attacker holds an auxiliary dataset $D_A$ and can obtain the response (image or text) from the API of the VLP model. Taking the outputs of API as the pseudo-labels of $D_A$, the paper constructs a surrogate dataset, ($D_A, API_{D_A}$), with paired information. Then a surrogate model is trained on the surrogate dataset. The experiments show that the surrogate models can achieve similar performance to the target models.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
1. The content of this paper is clear and easy to understand.
2. The experimental results prove that the proposed method can successfully steal the functionality of VLP models fine-tuned on image-text retrieval tasks.
3. IP Protection of deep learning models is an important issue to the community, but the concern to VLP models is rarely investigated. The proposed method shows that VLP models fine-tuned on image-text retrieval tasks can be stolen with a modest budget.

Weaknesses and Questions:
1. The proposed method is hardly innovative, and the experimental results are not surprising. The proposed mechanism for constructing a surrogate image-text retrieval dataset has no difference from that of the image classification task. Although VLP APIs can adopt both image and text as the query when compared to classification APIs that can only accept the image as a query, there are not many more accompanying challenges. Intuitively, VLP models that are fine-tuned on target tasks can achieve high performance, so the surrogate dataset is highly similar to the original train set. Although the paper reveals that VLP models that are fine-tuned on image-text retrieval tasks can be stolen, I am not sure whether this paper can bring new insights to the community.
2. As stated in the paper, VLP models have achieved promising performance on various vision-language tasks. However, the paper only concentrates on image-text retrieval. To my understanding, the proposed method can also be adopted for stealing VLP models fine-tuned on other tasks, like image captioning. What about the effectiveness of the proposed method on other V-L tasks?
3. It seems that the proposed method is not very query-efficient. As presented in Section 4.3, “only 10% $|D_F|$ queries gain an improvement of at least 6%”. From the perspective of reality, 10% of the training data is not a small quantity and is also hard to access. As presented in Table 4, there is an obvious performance degeneration when the auxiliary dataset and the original train set are in different distributions. What if reducing the size of the auxiliary dataset comes from a different distribution?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: clear and easy to understand.
Quality: modest
Novelty: marginal novelty.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper investigates model stealing attacks against VLP models fine-tuned on image-text retrieval tasks. The proposed method lacks novelty and contributes marginally to the community. More convincing experiments are needed.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This submission shows the stealing and defending from the CLIP model fine-tuned on two downstream tasks. It proposes the model stealing attack against the vision-language models. This experimental paper considers different dimensions of the model extraction attack: query efficiency, data used for stealing (two surrogate datasets: Flickr30K and MSCOCO), the architecture of the victim model, and the type of exposed API.

An interesting observation is that the attacks against image-to-text retrieval or text-to-image retrieval APIs lead to the similar performance of stolen copies, which implies that these two APIs leak a similar amount of information.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Main points:
1. Authors consider only fine-tuning while in real scenarios such models should be trained from scratch since the underlying encoders/models are not known. This is a very well-known result that stealing only the fine-tuned part is easy (e.g., Krishna et al. 2020).
2. Comparison to previous work on model stealing is rather non-existent. 

What is the meaning of the green dashed line in Figure 2? What is the Query Size (is it the fraction of the dataset used for stealing)? Are there only 8 data points reported in Figure 2 a? If so, the results can be represented as a table. 

This paper shows how to steal image-to-text and text-to-image models. It performs standard comparisons for 3 aspects: query efficiency, architecture type, and data type. The stolen fine-tuned model is trained in the same way as the fine-tuning is done for a victim. The results are expected. What are the novel insights in the experimental results? The fact that stealing from text or image API performs similarly is indeed interesting - however, it could be shown more about how the same embedding or different ones (for image and text) influence both stealing types. 

Related work is largely missing:

- The paper assesses a very simple method that is not considered as a defense against model stealing. The paper ignores the defenses based on watermarks (https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.11692 and https://proceedings.mlr.press/v162/dziedzic22a) and fingerprinting (https://openreview.net/forum?id=hvdKKV2yt7T and the follow-up for self-supervised models: https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.09024). 
- There were already papers that steal from the CLIP model and in general from self-supervised models from scratch: https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.11692 and https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.05889).
- The other work also shows that stealing to transformer-based models is better than extracting to CNN-based model architecture [1].

**References:**

[1] V. Battis and A. Penner, "Transformer-based Extraction of Deep Image Models," 2022 IEEE 7th European Symposium on Security and Privacy (EuroS&P), 2022.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Neat:

- Figure 1 - I suppose it should be: "In the left part, the victim" instead in the upper part, and respectively, "In the right part, the attacker" instead of in the below part.
- Presentations of results: e.g., the legends are the same in Figure 2 (a) and (b) - it could be shown once. The figure could be also squeezed vertically. 
- Conclusion: "building nonsensical texts generators." texts -> text
- "Although such attacks can be implemented in a wide range of realistic scenarios with little technical skill requiring," requiring -> required
- Table 6 should not be placed in the Conclusion section - where it does not belong to.
- This is minor: The metric Recall @ could be explained a bit more in terms of state-of-the-art, comparison to other models, etc. - which makes it more challenging to understand the paper fully while the work is purely experimental. The metric should be explained in the main paper a bit more than "the fraction of times the matched texts/images appear in the top-K retrieved results" or at least in the appendix since the understanding of the results hinges on it.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper is missing the related work. The work considers only stealing from a fine-tuned model and not the entire encoder. The experimental part could be improved.

content.title: Model Stealing Attacks Against Vision-Language Models
content.TL;DR: We propose the first model stealing attack against the vision-language models.
content.abstract: Vision-language models have flourished these years and are regarded as promising solutions to vision-language tasks. However, training vision-language models always requires enormous effort, making the models valuable intellectual properties (IPs). In this paper, we pioneer to propose the first model stealing attack against the vision-language models, the goal of which is to steal the functionality of the target models. Specifically, we target fine-tuned CLIP models with black-box access. We query the model to extract model information through either the text-to-image retrieval or the image-to-text retrieval API and then leverage the information to train a local copy of the target model. Experiments show the effectiveness of the model stealing attacks. We validate that our attacks are query-efficient, API-agnostic, data-agnostic, and architecture-agnostic, which broaden the attack scenarios. As a counterpart, we examine a defense based on the idea of out-of-distribution detection, which is impotent without strong assumptions. Our research pressures the unprotected release and prevalence of powerful vision-language models and appeals to the community that their IP protections, if not the least, cannot be less.
